title: MC1-04430
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): They are appealing a negative decision issued by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on June 18, 2021, after a virtual hearing that took place on March 16, 2021.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss this appeal. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Co-Appellant) are citizens of Mexico. They are appealing a negative decision issued by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) on June 18, 2021, after a virtual hearing that took place on March 16, 2021.

The Appellants fear the Co-Appellant's ex-boyfriend (XXXX or agent of harm) and his father who have ties to criminals. They allege that the Co-Appellant met XXXX sometime in XXXX of 2016, and that they became boyfriend and girlfriend in XXXX of 2017. The relationship ended in XXXX 2017, with the intervention of XXXX father. The Co-Appellant alleges that the agent of harm was controlling, as well as physically and emotionally abusive throughout the relationship.

They allege that the agent of harm started stalking the Co-Appellant and harassing her over the phone. On XXXX XXXX, 2019, XXXX called the Co-Appellant and issued death threats if she were to be with another man. The same day, he waited for her to return to her house and threatened her with a weapon. The Appellant reported the incident to the police on XXXX XXXX, 2019, in Morelos. However, the agent of harm, through email, told them that he knew about the denunciation and that the police worked for him. The Appellants moved to Mexico City on XXXX XXXX, 2019. On XXXX XXXX, 2019 the Co-Appellant received another email from XXXX, telling her that he knew they had now moved to Mexico City and issued death threats. Those emails were not sent from an email address carrying his name. The Appellant's sister suggested they leave Mexico for Canada where they could ask for protection. They left on XXXX XXXX, 2019, and claimed refugee status on XXXX XXXX, 2019.

The determinative issue before the RPD was credibility: both Appellants were found to be not credible and their allegations were, therefore, unfounded. Before the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD), the determinative issue remains the one of credibility.

I conclude that the RPD correctly found that the Appellants failed to establish their allegations on a balance of probabilities, and, therefore, that they would face a serious possibility of persecution based on their gender if they were to return to Mexico today.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
My role is to look at all the evidence, including the recording of the RPD hearing, and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1

The RPD found that the Appellants were overall not credible and that neither the psychological reports nor the gender guidelines could provide a basis to resolve the discrepancies identified in the evidence.

The Appellants submit that the RPD erred in its credibility assessment by disregarding the XXXX reports and conducted a microscopic analysis of the evidence. They also argue that the tribunal misapplied the gender guidelines. The RPD Was Correct in Finding Insufficient Credible Evidence that the Agent of Harm Existed

The RPD found that there was insufficient trustworthy evidence that XXXX existed. In reaching this finding, it considered that: (i) the police investigation file does not include the agent of harm's real name; (ii) no pictures of the agent of harm were submitted into evidence; (iii) Facebook is an untrustworthy source to confirm the agent of harm's identification; (iv) evidence of threats came from emails dated XXXX 2019, after their departure from Mexico, while no evidence was filed to corroborate alleged threats of 2017, which undermined their credibility as to having received threats and been harassed since XXXX 2017.

In her XXXX XXXX, 2021, sworn declaration, the Co-Appellant argues that she had destroyed all pictures, texts and messages from the agent of harm, as she wanted nothing to do with him anymore that could remind her of him. The RPD therefore erred in not taking this part of her testimony into account, as a victim of abuse. The Appellants contend that the RPD's finding about not providing a picture of the agent of harm to the Board to amount to an implausibility finding, ignoring the abused woman's perspectives and trauma. They argue that omitting the name of the agent of harm in the police report was due to trauma, which was not duly appreciated by the panel. Both Appellants argue that the tribunal further erred by not engaging into an analysis of the XXXX reports that corroborates the abuses they suffered as alleged in their Basis of Claim forms (BOC). They submit that those reports are objective, independent and third-party evidence that the RPD could not just dismiss without providing a reasoned opinion. They contend that the tribunal instead looked at their testimonies with a magnifying glass to find microscopic contradictions. They maintain that the psychological reports could explain the inconsistencies found by the panel.

The Appellants also submit that the panel appeared cold and insensitive to gendered issues, contrary to what is required by the Gender Guidelines. They reproached the RPD of not having considered their social, cultural, religious, and economic background in light of both the Gender Guidelines and the objective evidence of the National Documentation Package (NDP). They stressed that the studies show that memories are unreliable to report the facts, as two people can remember events differently. The RPD also ought to recognize the barriers to deliver a testimony in unfamiliar surroundings, intimidated by people in authority, while facing psychological difficulties and traumas, as well as cultural and language obstacles.

After having listened to the recording of the hearing, I find that the RPD member at all times adopted an appropriate tone with the Appellants, showing respect and empathy in light of the abuse allegations and acknowledging possible trauma. I therefore dismiss the Appellants' argument to the effect that the panel appeared cold or inappropriate, in violation of the Gender Guidelines.

As for the XXXX reports (Reports), the RPD mentioned them both in the decision and at the hearing, and specified having read and taken them into consideration.2 Contrary to the Appellants' arguments, the Reports are not independent or third-party evidence, since they are based on the facts reported by them to the psychologist. The Federal Court repeatedly reasoned: The problem with this kind of evidence, whether from psychologists, anthropologists or specialists in other disciplines, is that it depends on the facts reported by the person concerned. If the facts are not found to be credible, as in this case, the expert's view, however competent and well-intentioned, is generally no more valuable (Jele v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2017 FC 24 at para 50; Hajikhanov v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 1249 at para 15; Moussounda v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 506 at para 8).3 [emphasis added]

As noted by the RPD, the Reports reveal that the Appellants suffer from symptoms of XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX(XXXX), but they also state that their long-term and short-term memories did not seem impacted by the events and that their "thinking processes" were normal and coherent. It is therefore against this backdrop that I will review whether the RPD was correct when it reached its conclusions. Though the RPD could have cited more of the reports, the Appellants did not indicate which part of the professional opinion had not been duly considered by the member who underlined her acknowledgement of the trauma diagnosis in the course of the proceedings.

I believe that the RPD correctly found that the absence of the agent of harm's real name in the Police Report undermined the Appellants' credibility. I observe that, during the hearing, the Appellants submitted two contradictory explanations to justify this situation: (1) XXXX real name was known only by those closest to him; (2) using his real name would have brought them problems due to his connections with the police. I struggle to understand how, by using his alias under which he was generally known, it would have avoided them potential problems, as opposed to using his real name that he allegedly did not use publicly. Also, as pointed out by the RPD, if the Appellants were really looking for state protection, the authorities ought to know the identity of the agent of harm.

I take note of points 7.4, 7.5 and 8.5.2 of the new Gender Guidelines stating that XXXX can explain why the Appellants would be unable to provide a "chronological or coherent" testimony or that it could have an impact on memory, producing inconsistencies, omissions, and vagueness. However, as observed before, the Reports do not point at any difficulties the Appellants could face in this regard as a result of the diagnosis. Also, during the testimonies, they never reported having problems remembering details of the events or reporting them in a chronological manner. I was unable to observe any either.

On appeal, the Appellants now submit that their omission from using the agent of harm's real name was due to trauma that impeded on their ability to think rationally. I cannot accept this justification as reasonable. It seems that the Appellants adjust their position to address the concerns raised by the tribunal and use trauma as a cover-all justification. Also, as I already noted, the Reports stated that neither Appellants faced issues in their thinking patterns or memories, in spite of the XXXX diagnosis. I therefore dismiss this argument and rule that the RPD correctly concluded that the absence of the agent of harm's real name from the police report undermined their credibility regarding his existence.

I note that in her testimony, the Co-Appellant testified that she never had any photos of the agent of harm, not that she destroyed them because she did not want to have anything to do with him anymore, as reported in the RPD decision.4 I therefore agree that the RPD erred, but for misquoting the record, not for the reasons advanced by the Appellants. During the hearing, the member specifically asked whether the Co-Appellant destroyed the pictures of the agent of harm or whether she ever had any, and she confirmed the latter.5 The Co-Appellant's sworn declaration therefore contradicts her own testimony on this issue, which, in my view, further undermines her credibility regarding the very existence of the agent of harm.

I agree with the RPD reasoning that, in the world we live today, it is difficult to accept that the Co-Appellant, despite her seemingly legitimate wish not to be in contact with the agent of harm, was unable to recover a picture of him through different media platforms available either publicly or through her friends. If she felt that this was too difficult for her in light of her traumatic experience, her counsel, or someone close to her, could have undertaken this task. This argument is therefore dismissed, and I rule that the RPD correctly found that the absence of such evidence, in light of the circumstances prompting doubts as to the truthfulness of this allegation, further undermines the Appellants' credibility.

Regarding the threatening Facebook messages, the RPD gave no probative value to those documents. I agree with this position.6 I also note that the Co-Appellant testified to having blocked the agent of harm from contacting her on social media. It is thus questionable as to how, even under a new Facebook account, XXXX was able to message her directly using Facebook Messenger. It is well known that Facebook offers a series of features to protect one's privacy. One of them prevents from being directly contacted by outsiders (not listed as one's Facebook friends), without an express permission from the owner of the account. Another feature makes it difficult to be found on Facebook by non-friends. In any event, the evidence shows that the alleged agent of harm would have tried several times to contact her using the same account. While she did not respond, she did not immediately block him either, which is a security feature she knew well.7 This becomes even more puzzling when he was using his full last name "XXXX XXXX" and with whom she had "1 friend in common: XXXX XXXX XXXX". Finally, I find suspicious that the Co-Appellant's name does not appear on the Facebook Messenger screenshots. Since they are all dated after her arrival in Canada, she must have received them on her new Facebook account that is still in use. I understand that those questions were not directly put to the Co-Appellant at the hearing, however, considering her high level of education, her young age, the fact that she had been a Facebook user for years, and that the credibility of those documents were already at stake in this appeal, I believe that those concerns, without being determinative, add to those already raised by the RPD. I believe that it was reasonable to expect that the Co-Appellant, fearing for her life and of being located by the agent of harm even in Canada, would have known or learned how to use the Facebook privacy features so as to protect herself from potential security threats. In reaching this finding, I take note that she had used in the past her technological awareness to download an application conceived to alert the authorities through a panic button, as it is described in paragraph 30 of her narrative.

Finally, I agree with the RPD that, in the circumstances of this case, the lack of evidence to support the Appellants' allegations regarding the harassment through, inter alia, social media, undermines their credibility. I note that the Co-Appellant testified that she had been unable to submit into evidence earlier messages that she would have received from the agent of harm as she shut down her Facebook account before coming to Canada and that she could not retrieve the messages since she was unable to remember her "other email or password" to recover the account.

I believe that, in her BOC, the Appellant alleged that her daughter was harassed through social media, her friends and messages, all of which does not necessarily correspond to emails. However, I note that the emails filed into evidence to support the allegations of harassment were forwarded to her counsel in XXXX 2019. It is therefore questionable that the Co-Appellant, when she was gathering the evidence in support of her refuge claim in XXXX 2019, was unable to remember the information that would allow her to recover highly relevant evidence from her former Facebook account she had just closed a few months before. Considering the other credibility issues already confirmed, I am unable to give credence to this part of her testimony, either that she closed her Facebook account before arriving in Canada, or that she was unable to re-open it to gather the necessary evidence. I also observe that such evidence could have been conveyed through other means, such as sworn declarations of friends or family members, like her aunt. I am therefore of the opinion that the RPD correctly found that the Appellants' credibility was undermined by the lack of evidence regarding the alleged threats they faced from XXXX 2017 onwards. Other Inconsistencies

The RPD also rejected the evidence linking the agent of harms to drug traffickers because the Appellant failed to submit the results of her Internet research of 2017 revealing that the agent of harms' father and uncles were "into drug trafficking". The panel also identified an inconsistency between the police investigation file dated XXXX 2019 in which the Co-Appellant declared having received death threats for the past three years, while testifying having received those threats since XXXX 2017, so only two years prior to the investigative file. Finally, the RPD noted an inconsistency between the BOC narratives of the Appellants regarding the XXXX 2017 event that led to the breakup. The panel rejected the explanation provided by the Co-Appellant to the effect that the differences between her version and her mother's was due to a mistake in the translation. This undermined the Appellants' credibility to the effect that the XXXX 2017 events ever happened.

In her sworn declaration, the Co-Appellant argues that she and her mother remember the XXXX 2017 events differently, which is normal in her opinion. In the Appellant's sworn declaration submitted on appeal, she re-explained that "[she] had seen on the Internet about XXXX father having been detained in Venezuela", but could not find it again when she arrived in Canada. They repeat that the RPD erred in dissecting their testimonies to find errors as opposed to concentrating on what happened to them in light of their background and psychological report.

I note that during her testimony, the Co-Appellant reported the XXXX 2017 events as stated by her mother in her BOC.8 However, this stands in contrast with her recollection of the event as she described in her own BOC. In this written version, the Co-Appellant explained that she never went home that day until "hours later". She also said nothing about being taken back by XXXX father, an information she mentioned during her testimony. In any event, I dismiss the argument to the effect that the Appellants simply remembered the events differently than her mother, as it is irrelevant to the inconsistency between her written narrative and her testimony. Also, I find that the Co-Appellant is, again, adjusting her response to fit the concerns raised by the Tribunal, as she never mentioned anything to that effect prior to this appeal. I understand that the Co-Appellant seemed very upset during this portion of the hearing, however, this cannot explain why she would remember the events so differently in XXXX 2019, especially when she took the opportunity to amend this part of her BOC prior to the RPD hearing.

I also note that the Appellant testified to the effect that she found out on the Internet that XXXX father had been arrested in Colombia, not Venezuela as per her argument on appeal.9 Though it is possible that the same information was no longer available a few years later, if XXXX family member was so prominent in the drug trafficking world that he had been arrested internationally, it is reasonable to expect that other sources of information would be available today to substantiate this allegation. While having mistaken Venezuela for Colombia is not determinative in and of itself, the evidence as a whole is too weak to support the allegation that the agents of harms were related to international drug traffickers, namely cartels.

As for the inconsistency in the police report regarding the number of years the Co-Appellant received threats from the agent of harms, as pointed out by the RPD, it is only an additional inconsistency in light of the other credibility concerns raised. Even if this argument on appeal is granted, it will not affect the result.

Consequently, I find that the RPD correctly found that the Appellants were not credible and that therefore their central allegations to the claim had not been established on a balance of probabilities. This conclusion takes into account the diagnosis elaborated in the XXXX reports, as well as the Gender Guidelines. I would like to note that the extracts of the NDP cited by the Appellants do not assist in providing an evidentiary basis to the allegations submitted in the refugee claim.

Consequently, I find that the RPD correctly concluded that the Appellants would not face a serious possibility to be persecuted or that, on a balance of probabilities, that they would be personally subjected to a danger of torture or face a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if they were to return to Mexico.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
